item.title: Sterilizer equipment for CWM Maternity not working, another sterilizer being used but turnaround is slow
item.description: Serious concerns are being raised by some patients and their families as the sterilizer equipment for the CWM Maternity Hospital is not working. When asked by fijivillage News on the concerns being raised, CWM Hospital Medical Superintendent, Doctor Luke Nasedra confirms the maternity sterilizer is currently down, and this has been the case from last week.
item.content:encoded:
Serious concerns are being raised by some patients and their families as the sterilizer equipment for the CWM Maternity Hospital is not working.

When asked by fijivillage News on the concerns being raised, CWM Hospital Medical Superintendent, Doctor Luke Nasedra confirms the maternity sterilizer is currently down, and this has been the case from last week.

He says it was attended to by the technicians but unfortunately it still has not worked.

Doctor Nasedra says they have utilized another sterilizer in the hospital.

He says the turnaround is a bit slow and the team is working collaboratively to ensure they continue to deliver the services safely.

Doctor Nasedra confirms they are currently working on the final phase of the installation of a much bigger sterilizer which should be operational before the end of the year.

item.title: Fiji Deaf Association forgives USP students following traditional apology
item.description: The Fiji Deaf Association says it has forgiven the USP students involved in a viral video after a face-to-face traditional apology or matanigasau allowed members of the Deaf Community to better understand the apology and the emotion behind it. The USP Students Association, led by the President of the iTaukei Students Association Viliame Takayawa, presented a traditional i-soro to members of the De
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Deaf Association says it has forgiven the USP students involved in a viral video after a face-to-face traditional apology or matanigasau allowed members of the Deaf Community to better understand the apology and the emotion behind it.

The USP Students Association, led by the President of the iTaukei Students Association Viliame Takayawa, presented a traditional i-soro to members of the Deaf Community at the National Council for Persons with Disabilities Complex.

Two of the three students involved in the video were also present and personally apologised to members of the Deaf Community and other organisations that had gathered in solidarity.

Acting Fiji Deaf Association President Melita Delaibau says the face-to-face meeting was important because previous public apologies shared through social media and media reports were difficult for some Deaf people to fully understand without sign language interpretation.

Delaibau says meeting the students in person allowed members of the Deaf Community to understand the emotion behind the apology and that it was directed personally to them.

She says the community has now accepted the apology, forgiven the students and is ready to move forward.

Delaibau says the incident has also helped build a stronger relationship between USP students and the Deaf Community.

She says they now hope to see the students attend sign language classes and continue learning about Deaf culture and communication.

Delaibau is also urging people not to look down on deaf people or people with disabilities.

She says they have the same rights as everyone else, including the right to education and equal opportunities, and also have their own language and culture.

USPSA President Adi Talatoka Cama says the association is grate ful that the Deaf Community accepted the traditional apology.

Cama say s while the students did not intend to mock the Deaf Community, the association believed it was important to go beyond a public statement and apologise in person.

She says the process has been a learning experience for the students and the wider association.

Cama says they hope the incident will encourage people to learn from their mistakes, understand how their actions can affect others and focus on reconciliation.

She says the association is thankful that the Deaf Community received them with an open heart and has allowed both sides to move forward.

item.title: Concern grows for children left behind as parents work overseas
item.description: Parents leaving Fiji for employment opportunities overseas while their children remain in the country, is an emerging concern being highlighted by the Substance Abuse Advisory Council. Council Director Josua Naisele says they are now seeing situations where one parent, and in some cases both parents, take up employment opportunities overseas while their children remain in Fiji.
item.content:encoded:
Parents leaving Fiji for employment opportunities overseas while their children remain in the country, is an emerging concern being highlighted by the Substance Abuse Advisory Council.

Council Director Josua Naisele says they are now seeing situations where one parent, and in some cases both parents, take up employment opportunities overseas while their children remain in Fiji.

Naisele says this is another changing family situation, that needs attention when considering the wellbeing of children.

He says parental separation and divorce are already among the family issues affecting some children, while parents moving overseas for work is another situation they are now seeing.

Naisele says when parents leave the country for employment, it is important that children continue to receive proper care, guidance, attention and emotional support.

He says children need stability and people around them whom they trust and feel comfortable talking to about what they are going through.

Naisele says parents and guardians have an important responsibility to ensure children continue to feel loved, respected and supported even when their family circumstances change.

He says strong family connections are important because simply providing children with their material needs, does not necessarily mean all their emotional needs are being met.

Naisele says families need to understand what children are experiencing, and ensure they have someone they can turn to when they face difficulties.

He says maintaining a strong and supportive family environment remains important in helping children deal with changes at home, and the challenges they face as they grow up.
